title: Women Worry More About Mistakes on Male Teams
paragraphs: Everyone makes mistakes at work, but not everyone feels comfortable admitting them. According to a new study, women who work on teams made up mostly of men are less comfortable owning up to their errors than their male colleagues.

The study was conducted by Paris Will and Dr Grace Lordan of the London School of Economics and was published in October in the journal Frontiers in Organizational Psychology. The researchers surveyed 1,485 people working in the UK finance industry. Most of the participants were women, and about 44% worked on teams where at least 75% of members were men.

Participants were asked to imagine that they had made a moderately serious mistake at work. They then rated, on a scale of one to seven, how comfortable they would feel reporting it, how much they expected to be punished, and whether they saw mistakes as chances to learn.

Women on mostly male teams gave an average score of 5.46 for comfort in admitting mistakes, compared with 5.94 for men on the same teams. These women were also less likely to see mistakes as learning opportunities. They scored 4.20 on that measure, compared with 4.62 for women on other teams. Interestingly, men's attitudes changed very little depending on the makeup of their team.

However, after considering other factors such as job level and working hours, women did not expect to be punished more harshly than men. This suggests that the difference is about how safe people feel, rather than about actual company rules.
The researchers suggested some possible explanations, such as worrying about confirming negative stereotypes, but they did not test these ideas.
The study has some limitations. It was based on an imaginary situation rather than real mistakes, and the data was collected in 2020. It also shows a connection, not a cause.
